reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry ties the two proverbs together directly, reading the rod of correction in 22:15 as effective only while a child's character is still forming, and the incorrigible fool of 27:22 as one whose folly has already hardened past that window.

discrepancy.connective: Form-critical scholar R. N. Whybray argues Proverbs is an anthology of originally separate collections that were never redactionally harmonized, so a pair like this preserves genuinely rival ancient wisdom voices on whether character can be reformed rather than one settled doctrine.

skeptic.name: R. N. Whybray
skeptic.work: The Composition of the Book of Proverbs
skeptic.attribution: R. N. Whybray, The Composition of the Book of Proverbs, JSOTSup 168 (Sheffield: JSOT Press, 1994)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Solomon had said (Pro 22:15), The foolishness which is bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod of correction, for then the mind is to be moulded, the vicious habits not having taken root; but here he shows that, if it be not done then, it will be next to impossible to do it afterwards; if the disease be inveterate, there is a danger of its being incurable.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: MHC explicitly names Pro 22:15 by citation and states the age/inveteracy-based harmonization for why 27:22 says the fool's folly will not depart -- directly on this row's tension.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pair under the heading "Folly,--treatment" (two columns: "Folly remediable." / "Folly remediless."), p. 278, quoting Prov 22:15 and 27:22 side by side and resolving the tension with the identical age-based distinction MHC uses: "'Foolishness,' in the first text, is the incipient waywardness which belongs...to children, and may be corrected by suitable discipline. The 'fool' in the second text, is the grown-up fool, whose folly is past cure."
